questions.question: In 2 Samuel 1:1-16 (when an Amalekite brings Saul's crown claiming to have killed the wounded king) and again in 2 Samuel 4:5-12 (when Rechab and Baanah assassinate Saul's son Ish-bosheth in his bed and bring his head to Hebron), the messengers expect David to reward them handsomely. How does David respond both times, and why?
options: He promotes the messengers to generals in his army while publicly pretending to mourn.
He pays them silver out of the royal treasury but banishes them from Hebron.

He refuses to build his throne on political assassination or gloat over a fallen rivalâ€”executing the opportunists who thought murder would buy royal favor, and composing the Song of the Bow to honor Saul and Jonathan.
He sends the messengers to the Philistine lords in Gath as a peace offering.
questions.explanation: 2 Samuel 1 and 4 show why all twelve tribes eventually trusted David: in a world where new rulers rewarded the murder of rivals, David punished opportunistic assassins and genuinely mourned the man who had hunted him.

questions.question: In 2 Samuel 7, when a settled King David proposes to build a permanent cedar temple ('house') for the ark of God, how does God turn David's proposal upside down through the prophet Nathan?
options: God commands David to build the temple immediately and tax the twelve tribes to fund it.
Playing on the word 'house,' God declares that the Lord Himself will build David an enduring royal 'house'â€”a dynasty.
God rejects the idea of a temple permanently and orders the ark returned to Shiloh.
God tells David that his older brother Eliab's descendants will build the temple instead.
questions.explanation: 2 Samuel 7:11-16 is the bedrock of the Davidic Covenant: David offers to build God a physical house, and God responds by promising to build David an eternal dynasty ('house').

questions.question: In 2 Samuel 9, how does King David treat Jonathan's crippled son Mephibosheth?
options: He locks him in a prison
He makes him a palace servant
He welcomes him to his royal table
He sends him away across Jordan
questions.explanation: In 2 Samuel 9:7-13, keeping his promise to Jonathan, David restores all of Saul's land to Mephibosheth and seats him permanently at the king's own table like one of his sons.

questions.question: In 2 Samuel 11, after King David sleeps with Bathsheba and learns she is pregnant, why does his initial cover-up plan fail when he brings her husband Uriah home from the battlefront?
options: Uriah discovers a secret letter written by Bathsheba's father in the palace.
General Joab refuses to send Uriah back to Jerusalem from the siege of Rabbah.
Bathsheba immediately confesses the affair to the prophet Nathan at the palace gate.
Even when David gets Uriah drunk, Uriah refuses to sleep in the comfort of his home while his fellow soldiers camp in the field.
questions.explanation: 2 Samuel 11:8-13 exposes a devastating moral contrast: drunk Uriah the Hittite has more loyalty and integrity toward his fellow soldiers than sober King David, unwittingly foiling David's cover-up.

questions.question: In 2 Samuel 12, how does Nathan wake up David's conscience after his sin?
options: With a story about a stolen lamb
By bringing soldiers into the palace
By writing a letter to Joab
By hiding the royal gold crown
questions.explanation: In 2 Samuel 12:1-7, Nathan tells a story about a rich man who stole a poor man's single beloved lamb, drawing out David's outrage before saying, 'You are the man!'

questions.question: When we compare King Saul's confrontation with Samuel in 1 Samuel 15 (over sparing Amalekite sheep) with King David's confrontation with Nathan in 2 Samuel 12 (over adultery and murder), David's crime is far worseâ€”so what distinguishes David's response in 2 Samuel 12:13 from Saul's response in 1 Samuel 15:15-30?
options: David offers ten times more gold and silver sacrifices at the tabernacle than Saul offered at Gilgal.
David blames General Joab for Uriah's death, whereas Saul took full personal responsibility for sparing Agag.

While Saul deflects blame onto the troops, rationalizes his motives, and begs Samuel to 'honor me now before the elders of my people' to save public face, David offers zero excuses or spinâ€”answering in two Hebrew words: 'I have sinned against the Lord.'
Nathan had no authority to remove a king from office, whereas Samuel held legal veto power over the throne.
questions.explanation: Comparing 1 Samuel 15 and 2 Samuel 12 reveals the anatomy of true vs. false repentance: Saul is obsessed with image management before the crowd ('honor me before the elders'), whereas David owns his guilt unconditionally without a single excuse.

questions.question: Before launching his armed coup in 2 Samuel 15, how does David's son Absalom methodically 'steal the hearts of the men of Israel' over four years?
options: He wins a series of heroic military victories against the Philistines on the western border.
He lowers royal taxes by paying the national budget out of his own silver mines.
He stands early by the city gate, flatters every citizen with a lawsuit that their case is right, and sighs that if only he were judge he would give everyone justice.
He builds a magnificent stone temple in Hebron and invites all twelve tribes to worship there.
questions.explanation: 2 Samuel 15:1-6 is a textbook anatomy of political subversion: Absalom exploits an administrative bottleneck in his father's court, telling every plaintiff what they want to hear while undermining confidence in existing leadership.

questions.question: During his barefoot flight from Jerusalem in 2 Samuel 15:25-26 and 16:5-12, King David makes two counter-intuitive decisions: he orders the priests to carry the Ark of God back into the city rather than bringing it with him, and he stops Abishai from beheading Saul's relative Shimei as Shimei pelts the king with stones and curses. What posture unites both decisions?
options: David has lost all hope of ever returning to Jerusalem and is surrendering the throne permanently to Absalom.
David is afraid that Shimei's clan in Benjamin outnumbers his own royal bodyguard.
David believes the Ark of the Covenant is too heavy for the priests to carry across the Jordan River.

Under the chastening fallout of his own sin, David refuses to use the Ark as a political prop or silence a critic by forceâ€”submitting himself wholly to God's verdict ('Let him do to me what seems good to him').
questions.explanation: 2 Samuel 15:25-26 and 16:10-12 show David at his most spiritually mature in his lowest hour: unlike Eli's sons in 1 Samuel 4, he refuses to use the Ark as a talisman, and he accepts Shimei's humiliation with humble surrender to God's discipline.

questions.question: In 2 Samuel 24, why does David refuse to take Araunah's land for free?
options: The law banned gifts from strangers
He will not give costless offerings
He wanted to sell the land
His general warned him against it
questions.explanation: In 2 Samuel 24:24, David insists on paying full price for the threshing floor and oxen, declaring, 'I will not offer burnt offerings to the Lord my God that cost me nothing.'
